name: Azul
lede: Azul is simply the Spanish and Portuguese word for blue, traced by the Pigment Compendium to Arabic and Persian words for lapis lazuli.

sections.title: Blue, by way of lapis lazuli
sections.body: Azul is the ordinary Spanish and Portuguese word for blue, cousin to Italian *azzurro* and English *azure* [1]. The Pigment Compendium traces the whole family back through Old French *azur*, recorded in the eleventh century, to Arabic *al-lazward* and ancient Persian *lazhward*, words that meant lapis lazuli, the blue stone, before they ever meant a color [1]. Spanish writers also used a related phrase, *sangre azul*, "blue blood," for noble ancestry free of Moorish descent [2]. In Spanish art history, *azul baxo* named a low grade of azurite pigment [1]. ColorHub's library lists the bare word Azul as an English color name only from the 2010 xkcd crowd survey [3]. Its nearest named neighbor is [[royal-blue|Bright Blue]], with [[electric-blue|Electric Blue]] and [[royal-blue|Royal Blue]] close by, and its closer English cousin is [[azure]] [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our 23,781-painting archive holds this exact saturated blue covering at least one percent of its canvas, as photographed [5]. In printed English and Spanish the word's use has climbed steadily since 1920 and peaked by the 2010s, tracking general vocabulary rather than any single pigment or dye [6].

origin.named_after: the Spanish/Portuguese word for blue, from Arabic al-lazward ("lapis lazuli")

questions.q: The word "azul" and its relatives ultimately trace back to a word meaning what?
True or false: "sangre azul" (blue blood) originally referred to a visible vein color in everyone.

openers: "Azul" and "azure" share a root that once simply meant lapis lazuli.
